'''''Sanguisorba minor''''', the '''salad burnet''',<ref name=fsfed/> '''garden burnet''',<ref name=gardenia/> '''small burnet''',<ref name=fsfed/> '''burnet''' (also used for ''[[Sanguisorba]]'' generally),{{citation needed|date=March 2022}} '''pimpernelle''',{{efn|{{IPA|fr|pɛ̃.pʁə.nɛl}}}}<ref name=gardenia/> '''Toper's plant''',<ref name=gardenia/> and '''burnet-bloodwort''',<ref name=fsfed>{{cite book|last1=Fryer |first1=Janet L. |date=2008 |title=Sanguisorba minor |work=Fire Effects Information System, [Online] |publisher= U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory (Producer).|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/forb/sanmin/all.html |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref> is an edible [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plant in the family [[Rosaceae]]. It has ferny, toothed-leaf foliage; the unusual crimson, spherical flower clusters rise well above the leaves on thin stems.<ref name=gardenia/> It generally grows to {{Convert abbreviated|25-55|cm}} tall<ref name=NRCS/> (moisture-dependent; as short as 2 cm in dry areas).<ref name=fsfed/> The large, long (sometimes 1m/3-foot), [[taproots]] store water, making it<ref name=fsfed/> drought-tolerant.<ref name=fsfed/><ref name=NRCS_2002/>

It is evergreen to semi-evergreen;<ref name=NRCS/> in warmer climates grows all year around,<ref name=gworld/> and in cold climates it stays green until heavy snow cover occurs. Plants may live over 20 years, though 7–12 is more usual;<ref name=fsfed/> it lives longer if sometimes permitted to set seed.<ref name=NRCS/> Burnet flowers in early summer.

Subspecies include ''muricata'', ''minor'', and ''mongolii'' (the last from the Mediterranean).<ref name=fsfed/>

== Occurrence ==
Salad burnet is native to western, central and southern [[Europe]]; northwest [[Africa]], southwest [[Western Asia]]<ref name=itis>{{cite web | url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=25303 | title=Link to ITIS entry | access-date=May 1, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://eol.org/pages/626892/overview | title=Link to EOL entry | access-date=May 1, 2012}}</ref> and Siberia.<ref name=fsfed/> In Britain, it is not native, but has been naturalized since the 16th century.<ref name=gworld/> It has also naturalized in most of North America,<ref name=itis/> in South America, Australia, and New Zealand.<ref name=fsfed/> It is not generally [[invasive plants|invasive]], co-existing with other plants and increasing species diversity. As of 2008 it had been reported as invasive in just one place, a [[pasture]] in [[Wyoming]].<ref name=NRCS/><ref name=fsfed/> The variables controlling salad burnet spread in North America are poorly studied.<ref name=fsfed/>

In Europe it is found only in [[calcerous soil]]s (see [[limestone]]), and is most common on [[chalk soil]]s (see [[chalk]]) in England.<ref name=NRCS_2002/> In France, it grows on alluvial meadows, and in the south of France, on [[Kermes oak maquis]] (a [[Quercus coccifera]] shrubland ecosystem with siliceous soil) and [[garrigue]] (a shrubland ecosystem with calcareous soil). In Spain, it grows on silaceous soils.<ref name=fsfed/>

In North America the species is probably much less diverse, due to [[founder effect]]s and heavy selective breeding for forage value, including selection for cold-tolerance.<ref name=fsfed/> It grows in a variety of soil types, generally infertile, well-drained soils, including weakly saline and weakly alkaline or acidic soils.<ref name=fsfed/> In North America, it grows at a broad range of elevations.<ref name=NRCS/> It is cold- and frost-tolerant,<ref name=fsfed/> growing in USDA [[hardiness zone]]s 4a-8a,<ref name="toolbox">{{cite web |title=Sanguisorba minor (Burnet, Garden Burnet, Salad Burnet, Small Burnet)|series=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/sanguisorba-minor/ |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu |publisher=University of North Carolina |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref> but does not grow well in shade.<ref name=NRCS_2002/><ref name=gardenia/>  It grows well on slopes<ref name=gardenia/> and disturbed soil,<ref name=fsfed/> and is sometimes used to stabilize soil.<ref name=NRCS_2002/> The ''delar'' cultivar widely grown in North America does not grow in damp or flooding areas,<ref name=fsfed/><ref name=NRCS_2002/> and needs over {{convert|14|in|cm}} of precipitation per year.<ref name="plant_guide_1997">{{cite web |author=compiled by Daniel G. Ogle, Plant Materials Specialist, NRCS, Boise, Idaho.|title=MANAGEMENT AND USE OF Small Burnet |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmspgsami3dela.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215041802/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmspgsami3dela.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 15, 2017 |date=1997}}</ref><ref name=NRCS/>

=== Cultivation ===
It is grown in containers, [[wildflower meadow]]s, ornamental gardens, and [[kitchen garden]]s, usually in sunny or very slightly shady spaces with an equator-facing or west-facing aspect.<ref name=gworld/><ref name=gardenia/> In North America, it is grown on dry [[rangeland]]s. It is used for grazing, erosion control, post-fire weed control, [[firebreak]]s, and landscape rehabilitation.<ref name=NRCS/> Because it tends to stay green, it is considered fire-resistant.<ref name=NRCS_2002/>

=== Propagation ===
Salad burnet can carry both male and female flowers on the same plant; that is, it is [[monoecious]].<ref name=fsfed/>{{clarify|reason=none of the images look it...?|date=March 2022}}

Salad burnet generally does not flower or seed in its first year of life.<ref name=fsfed/> Grazing can prevent flowering, and [[ungulates|hooved animals]], [[rabbit]]s, [[hare]]s, [[rodent]]s, and [[grasshopper]]s may eat almost all of the seed in some areas, but plants can also sprout from rodents' seed caches.<ref name=fsfed/> The seeds are surrounded by a winged [[hypanthium]] until they germinate; the reason for the wings is unknown. Apart from being carried by animals, they might be dispersed by wind and water, which might account for the wings. In the wild, seeds survive in soil for decades, and despite the soil moisture, which tends to rot them, about half will still sprout; this is the natural gemination rate in Europe.<ref name=fsfed/> Salad burnet can spread fairly quickly by self-seeding.<ref name=NRCS_2002/> It can also be spread by division, and it can spread through rhizomes, but young plants are easy to pull up,<ref name=gardenia/> thought they develop taproots fairly rapidly.<ref name=fsfed/>

Seed is mature when hard and dark; commercially, it is harvested with a high [[combine harvester]] to selectively take the seed while leaving the herbage. Yield is {{convert|500|-|550|lb/acre|kg/hectare}} when irrigated, about a third that in drier conditions. commercial seed remains viable for several years if stored cool at 12 to 15 percent moisture,<ref name=NRCS/> and seed in a warehouse has shown no appreciable drop in viability after 25 years of storage.<ref name=fsfed/> Germination rates actually increase over three years of storage, and commercial seed usually has over 90% field germination rates, but both seed yields and germination rates are probably elevated in domestic species due to [[artificial selection]]. North American wild rates are not known.<ref name=fsfed/> Salad burnet establishes slowly, and so it is not grazed (nor expected to flower much) for the first year.<ref name=NRCS/>

In the wild, seed is buried an average of 10 cm or 4 inches deep. In a greenhouse experiment, germination peaked when seeds were set 6 cm (2.5 inch) deep.<ref name=fsfed/>

== Usage ==
=== Culinary ===
[[File:Kräuterbutter.JPG|thumb|Used in herb butter]]
Young burnet leaves are used as an ingredient in salads, dressings, sauces,<ref name=lima/> summer drinks,<ref name=gworld>{{Cite web|title=Sanguisorba minor|url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/plants/sanguisorba-minor/|access-date=2020-10-01|website=BBC Gardeners' World Magazine|language=en}}</ref> and in [[Bordeaux wine#"Claret" term|claret]].<ref>[[:File:Gardenology.org-IMG 2173 hunt08sep.jpg]]</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Compleat Herbal of Physical Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/gri_33125014247049/page/n5/mode/2up |author=Pechey, John |author-link=John Pechey |year=1707 |page=[https://archive.org/details/gri_33125014247049/page/n51/mode/2up 39] |publisher=London: Printed for R. and T. Bonwicke}} quote: "The green Herb is put into Wine, to chear the Heart; and it renders it very pleasant, by imparting an Aromatick Smell and Taste to it." </ref> It is also used to flavour vinegar, butter, and cream cheese.<ref name=NRCS_2002>{{cite web |last1=United States Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Center |series=Plant Guide|title=SMALL BURNET Sanguisorba minor Scop. Plant Symbol = SAMI3 |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmspg04840.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170212103500/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmspg04840.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 12, 2017|date=23 September 2002}}</ref>

It has a flavor described as "mildly [[cucumber]], a bit tart, a little hot"<ref name=lima>{{Cite book|last=Lima, Patrick.|title=Herbs : the complete gardener's guide|date=2001|publisher=Firefly|others=Forsyth, Turid.|isbn=1-55209-624-6|location=Willowdale, Ont.|oclc=64630388}}</ref> and is considered interchangeable with mint leaves in some recipes, depending on the intended effect. Typically, the youngest leaves are used, as they tend to become bitter as they age; old leaves are cut back to encourage new growth.<ref name=gardenia/>

Salad burnet was called a favorite herb by [[Francis Bacon]], was brought to the New World with the first English colonists, and was given special mention by [[Thomas Jefferson]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Betts |first1=Ewin Morris |title=Thomas Jefferson's Garden Book |date=1944 |publisher=The American Philosophical Society |page=480}}</ref> It declined in popularity as a kitchen herb, but as of 2022, is becoming more popular again, for food and as an ornamental.<ref name=gobot>{{cite web |title=Sanguisorba minor (salad burnet): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/sanguisorba/minor/ |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref>

=== Ornamental ===
[[File:Sanguisorba minor subsp. minor sl9.jpg|thumb|upright=3|Female flower ([[:File:Sanguisorba minor subsp. minor sl11.jpg|male flower]])]]
The unusual crimson, ball-shaped blooms are carried aloft on tall, thin stems, well above the ferny, toothed-leaf foliage.<ref name=gardenia/> The leaves are often considered more ornamental than the flowers,<ref name="gardenia"/> which are often removed to encourage more foliage growth.<ref name="toolbox"/><ref name=gardenia>{{cite web |title=Sanguisorba minor (Salad Burnet) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/sanguisorba-minor |website=Gardenia.net |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref> However, the cut flowers are used in floral arrangements.

=== For wild and domestic animals ===
The flowers provide nectar and pollen, and attract bees, butterflies, moths, and other pollinators and beneficial insects.<ref name=gworld/> It is classified as a moderate honeybee food in New Zealand, and as a good nectar producer in the United States.<ref name=NRCS/>

Salad burnet is good forage for wildlife and livestock, partly because it stays green for so long. Elk, deer, antelope and birds forage on the leaves and seeds. It provides cover for small birds, and it is used by the [[greater sage-grouse]]. It is planted on rangelands in western North America, including in [[pinyon-juniper woodland]]s, [[ponderosa pine]] forests, dry [[quaking aspen]] parklands, mountain grasslands, [[chaparral]], desert and mountain shrublands, and [[sagebrush steppe]]. After the first year, it is grazed roughly every 35 days, or whenever it is {{convert|12|in|cm}} tall, until it is half that height.<ref name=NRCS>{{cite web |author=USDA NRCS Idaho Plant Materials Program and National Plant Data Center |series=Plant Guide|title=SMALL BURNET Sanguisorba minor Scop. Plant Symbol = SAMI3 |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmcpg11634.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210034524/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/idpmcpg11634.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 10, 2017 |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]], Natural Resources Conservation Center |date=January 2013}}</ref>

=== Medicinally ===
{{More medical citations needed|section|date=March 2022}}
Salad burnet has in the past been used medicinally in Europe to control bleeding.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bown |first1=Deni |title=The Royal Horticultural Society New Encyclopaedia of Herbs & Their Uses |date=2002 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley Limited |location=London |isbn=0-7513-3386-7}}</ref>

Salad burnet has the same medicinal qualities as medicinal burnet (''[[Sanguisorba officinalis]]''). It was used as a tea to relieve diarrhea in the past.
